newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Mine workers flex their muscles.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mine workers flex their muscles.

text.p: Just two weeks after the end of a month long strike at the west's leading nickel producer Inco, mine workers at two other major facilities were set for a show of strength with their management.

Among other commodities coffee remained vulnerable to Brazilian weather talk, soyabeans roared ahead on Chinese buying talk while an Australian minister attempted damage limitation in the gold market.
Workers at Canada's Falconbridge Ltd, voted to give their negotiators a strike mandate to take into pay talks with management at the Sudbury, Ontario, nickel, copper and cobalt facilities.
This was seen as an attempt to win the same improved deal that workers at neighbours Inco Ltd, which produces the same metals, achieved by striking for most of June.
Nickel prices on the London Metal Exchange took a late $100 leap on the news to around $6,900 a tonne.
Management were optimistic "Our plan is to be done on time (August 1) and with a contract," Falconbridge's director of human resources Gerald Foley said.

In Portugal workers at Europe's biggest copper mine, the 100,000 tonne a year facility at Neves Corvo, stopped work in protest at the attempted imposition of a Sunday shift which management claimed was essential if the mine was to stay competitive.

There was no immediate reaction in London Metal Exchange copper prices as warehouse stocks of the metal are currently building-up but as the Portuguese mine supplies European smelters with feed material, traders were keeping a close watch on the situation.
The price drifted lower to end the day at $2,368 a tonne with traders looking for buyers to step in at around $2,350.
On the coffee market trader talk of the possibility of a cold front bringing cooler temperatures to Brazil helped prices to firm at one stage.

But U.S. based forecaster Weather Services Corp soon downplayed the talk saying "a high pressure will continue to dominate the coffee belt during the next seven days preventing any cold air from entering the region,"
London robusta coffee futures ended the day trading at $1,785, up just eight dollars from Monday.
In Chicago soyabean futures charged higher as dealers spread talk that China had purchased old and new crop this week and that trade houses were in the market to cover the business.
On the Board of Trade July futures reached 30 cents a bushel higher at $7.63.

The gold market, battered by several days of selling by disillusioned investors, showed relative stability as Australia, the main culprits behind the fall, attempted to smooth over the effect that the news of their 167 tonnes gold sale had on the market last week.
Trade minister Tim Fischer said there was still a future in gold mining and that demand for the metal would increase in time.
Speaking in Durban, South Africa, he said "The Australian government would like to encourage the future of gold mining."
He noted that it was the Australian central bank's decision to sell two-thirds of its gold reserves this year and not the government.
On the London bullion market the gold price crept back above $320 having been down to a near 12 year low below $315 on Monday.
